# 1 Historical Periods of Music

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide organises every period the same way: a **key word**, the historical
context, the characteristic style, the forms and genres, the composers to know,
and a listening focus. The key word is the shortest possible summary of the
period — learn those first and the rest of each period hangs off them.

Read the periods as a sequence rather than as five separate lists. The texture
alone tells a story: one line in the Middle Ages, several equal lines through the
Renaissance and Baroque, then a single tune with accompaniment from the Classical
period onwards.

## Middle Ages (c. 500–1400)

**Key word: dark.**

**Context.** The period is dominated by the Church, and music served religious
ritual. The practice set sums the whole period up as religious and sacred, built
on church modes and written in the new notation.

**Style.**

- **Monophony** — a single melodic line, as in Gregorian chant.
- **Neumes** — early notation, developed as the notation for Gregorian chant.

**Forms and genres.** **Plainchant**, also called Gregorian chant: sacred songs
in Latin. The practice answers add that it was the official music of the Roman
Catholic Church, which is the reason the guide gives for it being the period's
one central genre.

**Key composer.** **Hildegard of Bingen** — a mystic nun and a prolific composer.

**Listening focus.** A chant-like quality; **modal scales** (Ionian, Dorian,
Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian); and a lack of steady beat.

## Renaissance (c. 1400–1600)

**Key word: humanism.**

**Context.** The rise of secularism, and the invention of the printing press. The
practice answers describe the period as more secular but still mostly sacred and
still modal, with harmony beginning to develop — and place it alongside realism
and linear perspective in the visual arts of the same moment.

**Style.**

- **Polyphony** — interweaving independent lines.
- **Word painting** — the music literally illustrates the lyrics. The guide's
  example is a setting of "rise rise rise rise" in which each "rise" is one
  semitone higher than the last; the practice answers give the same idea as
  "ascending" set to rising pitch.

**Genres.**

| Genre | Sacred or secular | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Mass** | Sacred | Polyphonic (many voices simultaneously) or plainchant |
| **Motet** | Sacred | A choral composition and a standalone piece, polyphonic, freer than the Mass and not always for worship |
| **Madrigal** | Secular | Vocal secular music |

**Key composers.** **Josquin des Prez**, who wrote motets, and **Palestrina**, who
wrote masses. The practice set adds **Weelkes** to the same list.

**Listening focus.**

- **Clarity of text.**
- **Imitative texture** — a polyphonic texture in which one voice or part imitates
  the melody of another voice or part, usually at a slightly later time.
- **Modal harmony** — no structural harmony such as V–I, but still a tonal centre,
  namely the mode.

Clarity of text and word painting belong together: both are ways of making the
music serve the words, which is what the period's humanism amounts to in
practice.

## Baroque (1600–1750)

**Key word: absolutism.**

**Context.** The dramatic arts, with their drastic contrasts of colour and their
characters in bloody motion; Versailles as the centre of music; and the
Counter-Reformation.

**Style.**

- **Unity of mood** — maintaining a constant emotional atmosphere.
- **Rhythmic drive** — a strong sense of momentum, usually maintained by drums or
  bass.
- **Basso continuo** — a continuous bassline played by one instrument, which can
  change and vary.
- **Terraced dynamics** — abrupt shifts between loud and soft.

**Key forms and genres.**

| Form | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fugue** | A musical structure: counterpoint with subject, answer, exposition, development and coda |
| **Concerto grosso** | Dialogue between the soloists (**concertino**) and the orchestra (**ripieno**) |
| **Opera** | A dramatic work or story, mostly sung, with orchestral accompaniment |
| **Oratorio** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra, choir and soloists |
| **Cantata** | A vocal composition with instrumental accompaniment, sacred or secular |
| **Toccata** | Free-flowing and improvisational, for organ or harpsichord |

The practice set lists **ritornello** alongside opera, oratorio, cantata and
toccata as a Baroque form. Neither the review guide nor the practice answers
define it, so learn it as a name on that list.

**Key composers.** **J.S. Bach**, famous for fugues; **G.F. Handel**, for the
"Hallelujah" chorus from *Messiah*; **Vivaldi**, for *The Four Seasons*;
**Monteverdi**; and **Pachelbel**, for *Canon in D*.

**Listening focus.**

- **Harpsichord** — a piano, except that the strings are plucked.
- **Ornamentation** — additional decorative elements, such as trills.
- **Continuous melody** — an uninterrupted flow.
- **Contrapuntal complexity** — elaborate use of counterpoint, meaning two or more
  melodic lines at the same time.

## Classical (1750–1820)

**Key word: enlightenment.**

**Context.** Enlightenment ideals — balance, clarity, form.

**Style.**

- **Homophony** — melody with accompaniment, that is, with harmony.
- **Balanced phrases** — a structure of two or more **phrases** (musical sentences
  that convey ideas) of equal length and similar tension.
- **Simple harmony** — two or more notes played together pleasingly, for example
  triads.
- **Clear cadences** — cadences with a clear conclusion: **authentic** (V–I) and
  **plagal** (IV–I).

Balance, clarity and form are exactly what those four features deliver, so the key
word is not decoration here: it names the thing the style was built to produce.

**Key forms and genres.**

| Form | Description |
|---|---|
| **Sonata form** | Exposition – Development – Recapitulation |
| **Symphony** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra; fast–slow–dance–fast |
| **Concerto** | A musical composition for one solo instrument |
| **String quartet** | Two violins, a viola and a cello |
| **Zu 2** | Two instruments play in unison |

**Key composers.** **Haydn**, the father of the string quartet and of the
symphony; **Mozart**, a prodigy, famous for his forty-one or so symphonies; and
**early Beethoven**. The practice answers call these the three giants: Haydn,
Mozart and Beethoven. The guide prints "nine symphonies" for Mozart here; that
is an error — nine is Beethoven's number, and Mozart wrote around forty-one.

## Romantic (1820–1900)

**Key word: individualism.**

**Context.** Nationalism and the Industrial Revolution.

**Themes.** Love, death, nature, the supernatural, exoticism.

**Musical features.**

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Program music** | Music that tells a story — for example *Symphonie fantastique* |
| **Rubato** | Speeding up and slowing down, with the overall duration left intact |
| **Expanded orchestration** | Increasing the size of the orchestra and the types of instrument in it |
| **Virtuosity** | Extreme technical skill — Paganini and Liszt |
| **Self-expression** | Composers tried to express their inner feelings through the music they created |

Program music and self-expression are the two features that follow directly from
the key word: both make the individual — a story, or the composer's own feeling —
the subject of the piece.

### Key composers

**Beethoven (late)** lost his hearing and became much more Romantic, expressing
his frustration through his music. He is the one composer the guide lists twice,
early under Classical and late under Romantic.

**Chopin** was Polish and physically weak, and wrote **nocturnes** — quiet, calm,
beautiful pieces. He is known as the poet of the piano.

**Liszt** was a pianist with big hands, a handsome womaniser who played difficult
pieces for fun.

**Berlioz** wrote unconventional music. He fell in love and wrote *Symphonie
fantastique*, in which the protagonist kills the woman he loves, goes to hell, and
meets her there.

**Brahms** was conservative and German, and was close friends with Clara Schumann.

**Tchaikovsky** was the Russian master of ballet — *The Nutcracker*, *Swan Lake* —
and was gay.

**Mendelssohn** was a devoted admirer of Bach, took advice from his sister Fanny,
and died at 38 from overwork.

**Schubert** was a hard-working admirer of Beethoven who wrote **Lieder** — art
songs, settings of a poem to music, such as *Erlking*.

**Richard Wagner** was German, hated Jews, and was a favourite of Hitler. He
used the **leitmotif**: a musical theme that suggests a person, an idea or an
event. The guide prints "Hungarian" here; that is an error — Wagner was German.

**Puccini** was Italian and worked in **verismo**, operas that portrayed real
people. *La Bohème* shows the real, difficult life of musicians, philosophers and
playwrights, and has soaring melodies.

**Listening focus.** Rich harmonies, dynamic contrasts, expressive melodies, and
experimenting with dissonance.

## The Modern era and the "isms" (1900–present)

**Context.** Two world wars, technology, global influence, and philosophical
shifts.

Where the earlier periods each have one dominant style, the modern era splits into
parallel movements, and the guide expects you to tell them apart by a single
distinguishing trait each.

### Impressionism

**Inspiration.** Claude Monet's painting *Impression: Sunrise*.

**Musical traits.**

- Whole-tone, pentatonic and modal scales.
- Colour and texture valued over clear form.
- Extended chords (9ths, 13ths) and floating rhythms.

**Key composers.** **Claude Debussy** (*Clair de Lune*) and **Maurice Ravel**.

### Primitivism

**Inspiration.** Folk art, tribal rhythms, prehistoric themes.

**Traits.**

- Savage rhythms.
- **Ostinatos** — short, repetitive musical phrases, typically at the same pitch
  or in the same rhythm.
- **Polytonality** — two or more keys or tonal centres used simultaneously.
- **Harsh dissonance** — exactly what it sounds like.
- **Simple motives** — short, recognisable ideas, such as the *Mission Impossible*
  theme.

**Key work.** Stravinsky's *The Rite of Spring*.

### Expressionism

**Themes.** Inner anxiety, nightmares, alienation. The practice set describes the
result as music that is often anxiety-inducing and spooky.

**Traits.** **Atonality**, extreme dissonance, and **Sprechstimme** — spoken
singing.

**Technique.** The **twelve-tone system**: serialism using tone rows. The practice
answers pair the twelve-tone system directly with atonality, which is how the two
terms relate — the system is the method, atonality the result.

**Key composers.** Schoenberg, Berg, Webern.

### Minimalism

**Traits.** Repetition, gradual change, and a steady pulse.

**Composers.** **Steve Reich** (*Clapping Music*) and **Philip Glass**.

### Electronic and chance (aleatoric, indeterminate) music

**Traits.** Synthesizers, tape loops, ambient textures, and **chance** — luck and
randomness as part of the composition.

**Figures.**

- **John Cage** (*4′33″*) — a music professor; his work asks what music is.
- **Varèse** (*Poème électronique*) — a pioneer of electronic music.
- **Kraftwerk** — pioneers of electric-synth, techno and electronic dance music.

### Telling the isms apart

The practice set is a matching exercise, and its answers amount to a checklist of
the one clue that identifies each movement.

| Clue | Movement |
|---|---|
| Repetition with gradual changes | Minimalism |
| An example would be Steve Reich's *Clapping Music* | Minimalism |
| Pentatonic, modal and whole-tone scales | Impressionism |
| Key figure: Claude Debussy | Impressionism |
| Some elements determined by chance | Electronic and chance music |
| Tape loops and synthesizers | Electronic and chance music |
| Prehistoric themes and tribal rhythms | Primitivism |
| Polytonality | Primitivism |
| The 12-tone system (atonality) | Expressionism |
| Often anxiety-inducing and spooky | Expressionism |

The practice answers mark polytonality as expressionism, but the review guide
lists polytonality among the traits of primitivism and does not give it to
expressionism at all; the table above follows the review guide.

## The periods side by side

The practice set opens with this table as a fill-in-the-blank exercise, so it is
worth being able to reproduce from memory.

| Period | Starts | Prominent texture | Key word |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | ~500 | Monophonic | Dark |
| **Renaissance** | ~1400 | Polyphonic | Humanism |
| **Baroque** | ~1600 | Mostly polyphonic | Absolutism |
| **Classical** | ~1750 | Homophonic | Enlightenment |
| **Romantic** | ~1820 | Homophonic (mostly) | Individualism |

| Period | Composers to name | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | Hildegard of Bingen | Religious, sacred; neumes as early notation; church modes |
| **Renaissance** | Josquin des Prez, Palestrina, Weelkes | More secular but mostly sacred, and modal; harmony development; realism and linear perspective in art; word painting |
| **Baroque** | J.S. Bach, Handel, Vivaldi, Monteverdi, Pachelbel (*Canon in D*) | Terraced dynamics, basso continuo, unity of mood, rhythmic drive, dramatic art |
| **Classical** | The three giants: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven | Balanced phrases, simple harmony, clear cadences |
| **Romantic** | Chopin, Liszt, Berlioz, Brahms, Tchaikovsky | Love, death, nature, the supernatural, exoticism |

| Period | Forms to name |
|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | Plainchant (Gregorian chant) |
| **Renaissance** | Mass (sacred), motet (sacred), madrigal (secular) |
| **Baroque** | Fugue, concerto grosso, opera, oratorio, cantata, toccata, ritornello |
| **Classical** | Sonata form, symphony, concerto, string quartet |
| **Romantic** | Program music, rubato, expanded orchestration, virtuosity |

## A note on the listening material

Each period in the guide ends with a **listening focus** rather than a named
recording, so everything the guide asks you to recognise is described in words and
is reproduced above. Where a specific piece is named — *Symphonie fantastique*,
*Clair de Lune*, *The Rite of Spring*, *Clapping Music*, *4′33″* — the guide gives
the title and nothing more, so learn the title and the trait it illustrates rather
than expecting a description of the sound.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Monophony** | A single melodic line, as in Gregorian chant |
| **Neumes** | Early notation, the notation used for Gregorian chant |
| **Plainchant (Gregorian chant)** | Sacred songs in Latin; the official music of the Roman Catholic Church |
| **Modal scales** | Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian |
| **Polyphony** | Interweaving independent lines |
| **Word painting** | Music that literally illustrates the lyrics |
| **Mass** | A sacred genre; polyphonic (many voices simultaneously) or plainchant |
| **Motet** | A sacred choral composition; a standalone piece, polyphonic, freer than the Mass and not always for worship |
| **Madrigal** | Vocal secular music |
| **Imitative texture** | A polyphonic texture in which one voice or part imitates the melody of another, usually at a slightly later time |
| **Modal harmony** | Harmony with no structural progressions such as V–I, but still with a tonal centre — the mode |
| **Unity of mood** | Maintaining a constant emotional atmosphere |
| **Rhythmic drive** | A strong sense of momentum, usually maintained by drums or bass |
| **Basso continuo** | A continuous bassline played by one instrument, which can change and vary |
| **Terraced dynamics** | Abrupt shifts between loud and soft dynamics |
| **Fugue** | A musical structure: counterpoint with subject, answer, exposition, development and coda |
| **Concerto grosso** | Dialogue between soloists and orchestra |
| **Concertino** | The group of soloists in a concerto grosso |
| **Ripieno** | The orchestra in a concerto grosso |
| **Opera** | A dramatic work or story, mostly sung, with orchestral accompaniment |
| **Oratorio** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra, choir and soloists |
| **Cantata** | A vocal composition with instrumental accompaniment, sacred or secular |
| **Toccata** | A free-flowing, improvisational piece for organ or harpsichord |
| **Harpsichord** | A piano, except that the strings are plucked |
| **Ornamentation** | Additional, decorative elements such as trills |
| **Continuous melody** | An uninterrupted flow of melody |
| **Counterpoint** | Two or more melodic lines at the same time |
| **Contrapuntal complexity** | Elaborate use of counterpoint |
| **Homophony** | Melody with accompaniment, that is, with harmony |
| **Phrase** | A musical sentence that conveys an idea |
| **Balanced phrases** | A structure of two or more phrases of equal length and similar tension |
| **Simple harmony** | Two or more notes played together pleasingly, for example triads |
| **Authentic cadence** | A cadence with a clear conclusion: V–I |
| **Plagal cadence** | A cadence with a clear conclusion: IV–I |
| **Sonata form** | Exposition – Development – Recapitulation |
| **Symphony** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra; fast–slow–dance–fast |
| **Concerto** | A musical composition for one solo instrument |
| **String quartet** | Two violins, a viola and a cello |

| **Program music** | Music that tells a story |
| **Rubato** | Speeding up and slowing down, with the overall duration left intact |
| **Expanded orchestration** | Increasing the size of the orchestra and the types of instrument in it |

# 2 Instruments and the Orchestra

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Instrument families

The practice set asks for **four instrument families** and answers **string,
woodwind, brass and percussion**. The same practice set then asks you to sort
individual instruments into six labels — the four families plus **keyboard** and
**electronic** — and the review guide lists all six groups together. Learn four as
the answer to "how many families", and six as the set of labels you sort
instruments into.

### Strings

Violin, viola, cello (violoncello), double bass, harp.

Played with a bow (**arco**) or plucked (**pizzicato**).

### Woodwinds

Flute (*flauto*), oboe (*oboi*), clarinet (in B♭), bassoon (*fagotti*),
contrabassoon.

Tone is produced via a **vibrating air column**.

### Brass

Trumpet (in B♭), French horn (in F, written as C, *corni*), trombone
(*tromboni*), tuba (in C or B♭). The guide glosses the trombone as *trombe*
here; that is an error — *trombe* is the Italian for trumpets, and *tromboni* is
the Italian for trombones.

The lips buzz into a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

### Percussion

- **Pitched:** timpani, xylophone.
- **Unpitched:** snare drum, cymbals.

### Keyboards

Piano (strings struck), organ, harpsichord.

The guide's own description of the harpsichord in the Baroque period is the
distinction to hold onto here: it is a piano except that the strings are plucked
rather than struck.

### Electronic

Synthesizers, samplers.

### Sorting practice

The practice set gives eighteen instruments to label. Its answers are worth
reading straight through, because most of the labelling is settled by the family
descriptions above rather than by memory.

| Instrument | Family | Instrument | Family |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trumpet | Brass | Piano | Keyboard |
| Harpsichord | Keyboard | Double bass | String |
| Flute | Woodwind | French horn | Brass |
| Organ | Keyboard | Tuba | Brass |
| Bassoon | Woodwind | Cello | String |
| Violin | String | Synthesizer | Electronic |
| Trombone | Brass | Harp | String |
| Clarinet | Woodwind | Viola | String |
| Oboe | Woodwind | Sampler | Electronic |

## The orchestra

**Seating.** Strings at the front, woodwinds in the centre, brass at the back,
percussion at the rear. The practice set asks these four as separate questions —
front, centre, back, rear — so the four positions have to be kept in that order.

Modern orchestras often include over 90 musicians.

## How the orchestra changed

| Period | The orchestra |
|---|---|
| **Baroque** | Small, harpsichord-centred ensembles |
| **Classical** | Balanced, with winds used in pairs, and less bass |
| **Romantic** | Larger, with added instruments (tuba, cymbals, harp) and an expanded size of the existing parts of the orchestra |
| **Modern** | Expanded percussion, exotic instruments, electronics |

The Romantic line here is the same fact as **expanded orchestration** in the list
of Romantic features: the period's taste for a bigger sound and its bigger
orchestra are one development described twice.

**Examples.** The guide names one work per stage:

- Haydn's Symphony No. 31 — Classical
- Wagner's *Ride of the Valkyries* — Romantic
- Stravinsky's *The Rite of Spring* — Modern

These are listening examples. The guide prints the titles and the period label
only, with no description of what to listen for in each, so treat them as three
titles to match to three stages of the orchestra's growth.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arco** | Playing a string instrument with the bow |
| **Pizzicato** | Plucking a string instrument |
| **Strings** | Violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp; played with a bow or plucked |
| **Woodwinds** | Flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, contrabassoon; tone produced by a vibrating air column |
| **Brass** | Trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba; the lips buzz into a cup-shaped mouthpiece |
| **Percussion** | Pitched (timpani, xylophone) and unpitched (snare drum, cymbals) instruments |
| **Keyboards** | Piano (strings struck), organ, harpsichord (strings plucked) |
| **Electronic** | Synthesizers and samplers |

# 3 Transposing

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **transposing instrument** does not sound the note that is written for it. The
guide's clearest statement of the problem is the clarinet, trumpet and cornet:
when the player sees a C on the score, it is actually a B♭ that comes out when
they blow it. Transposing is the four-step procedure for getting from one to the
other.

## The procedure

1. **Understand the key of the instrument.** This is the note that sounds when the
   instrument plays a written C, and it is what the tables below record.
2. **Find the interval between that key and concert pitch (C).**
3. **Move all the notes in the piece by that interval.**
4. **Adjust the key signature** to match your new transposed key.

Steps 2 and 3 are why step 1 matters: the instrument's key is not a label to
memorise on its own, it is the thing you measure the interval from.

## Keys of the instruments

The guide groups the instruments by their key and gives an interval for some of
them. Where the interval column is empty, the guide names the instrument in that
key but does not print the interval.

| Key | Instruments | Interval the guide gives |
|---|---|---|
| **B♭** | Clarinet, trumpet, cornet | — (a written C sounds as B♭) |
| **F** | French horn, English horn, alto clarinet | English horn: a perfect fifth (P5) lower |
| **E♭** | Alto saxophone, baritone saxophone, E♭ clarinet | Alto saxophone: a major sixth (M6) lower. Baritone saxophone: a major sixth plus an octave (M6 + P8) lower. E♭ clarinet: a minor third (m3) higher |
| **G** | Alto flute | A perfect fourth (P4) lower |

Two of these run in the less obvious direction and are worth marking: the **E♭
clarinet sounds higher** than written, not lower, and the **baritone saxophone**
is the only instrument given an interval larger than an octave.

## Degrees of the scale

The practice set also asks for the names of the degrees of the scale, filling in
the gaps in a printed sequence. Its answer key gives them in this order:

| Degree | Name |
|---|---|
| 1 | Tonic |
| 2 | Supertonic |
| 3 | Mediant |
| 4 | Subdominant |
| 5 | Dominant |
| 6 | *(the answer key prints "subdominant" a second time)* |
| 7 | Leading tone |

The answer key repeats "subdominant" for both the fourth and the sixth degree;
since it names the fourth degree the subdominant in the sequence itself, go by the
positions and treat the sixth as the one name the guide does not supply.

## What the guide does not print

Steps 3 and 4 describe operations on a piece of notation — moving every note,
then rewriting the key signature — but the guide sets out the procedure without a
worked transposition and without a notated example to work it on. Practise the
steps on music you already have in front of you; there is no exercise supplied
here to check yourself against.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transposing** | Moving all the notes of a piece by an interval and adjusting the key signature to the new key |
| **Key of an instrument** | The pitch that actually sounds when the instrument plays a written C — B♭ for the clarinet, trumpet and cornet, F for the French horn, and so on |
| **Concert pitch** | C; the reference the instrument's key is measured against |
